newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Parliament defies Yeltsin on Nazi art-agencies.
newsitem.headline: Parliament defies Yeltsin on Nazi art-agencies.

text.p: Russia's parliament appears to have overruled a presidential veto on a draft law asserting Russian ownership of art works seized from Nazi Germany during World War Two, news agencies reported on Tuesday.
The State Duma lower chamber has already overturned President Boris Yeltsin's veto on the draft law.

Interfax news agency quoted sources at the Federation Council upper chamber as saying more than 135 of its deputies had also voted to overrule the president, well above the required threshold of 119, or two thirds of the chamber.
Itar-Tass news agency gave a similar figure.
Art works taken from the Nazis during the war include a priceless Gutenberg bible and paintings by impressionists Claude Monet and Henri Matisse.
A spokeswoman for the Federation Council could not comment on the news agency figures.
She said official figures would only be available on Wednesday when deputies meet for a regular session. Council members voted by post on the controversial issue.

If the result of the vote is confirmed on Wednesday, Yeltsin must sign the draft law within seven days, unless he appeals against it to the Consitutional Court. His representatives in parliament have already said Yeltsin would appeal.
The art has become a pressing issue, half a century after World War Two, because Russia has admitted holding many more art trophies than it previously acknowleged.
The Soviet government had hidden them in the basements of museums and other secret vaults.
Many Russians view the art as compensation for the wartime suffering of the Soviet people and for the many Russian treasures destroyed in the German invasion.
But Germany, Russia's biggest economic partner in the West and a strong political supporter, is lobbying hard for the pictures to be returned.

Yeltsin argued, when he used his veto, that the ownership bill breached international laws, would complicate Russia's relations with many states and could prevent Moscow from recovering artworks taken from the Soviet Union during the war.
